newsitem.title: UK: Oil slips as speculators exit U.S. gasoline.
newsitem.headline: Oil slips as speculators exit U.S. gasoline.

text.p: Oil prices on Thursday sank sharply, wiping out gains posted the day before as a rally on the gasoline market in the United States went into reverse.
London September Brent crude futures dipped 41 cents to $18.56 a barrel putting prices back into the range in place since early June.
Oil prices, sensitive during the summer months to demand for gasoline in the U.S., have found support from rising demand and hiccups in refinery operations.
Speculators, active buyers of the New York gasoline contract in the past week, scrambled to close positions before the August contract expired.
Prices fell nearly four cents a gallon to 66.2 cents knocking a big hole in the 10-cent gains posted since last Wednesday.

Output disruptions and strong demand have tightened prompt supply of gasoline. Data released by the American Petroleum Institute (API) recorded a feverish 8.7 million barrels per day (bpd) implied gasoline demand over the past month.
Tosco Corp shut down a gasoline producing unit at its 250,000 bpd Bayway refinery on Wednesday after detecting a leak, a source close to the refinery said.
The New Jersey facility normally produces 130,000 bpd of gasoline and houses the largest catalytic cracking unit in the world.
News from the United Nations also helped the fall, brokers said.

The U.N. was expected to approve Iraq's aid-distribution plan, the final hurdle to a resumption of Iraqi exports under the U.N. food-for-oil deal, by the weekend, well-placed sources at the organisation said.
"We have said that we would approve it by the end of July and I would say give or take a day or so we will have it done," said a senior U.N. official involved in the review of the deal.
Iraq has made approval of the aid plan a condition of restarting oil exports under the "oil-for-food" deal.
Once it is approved, Iraq must submit for approval by the U.N.'s overseers a price formula and oil sales contracts, a process that is expected to take no more than a few days.

The scheme allows Iraq to sell slightly more than $2 billion of oil over 180 days in two equal installments. The clock started ticking on June 8, which means Iraq must sell $1 billion of oil by September 5 or forego some of its allotment.
Though Iraq officials had said it was looking for the U.N. to start the clock ticking from the date of approval of the aid plan, Baghdad appeared to drop that issue on Wednesday.
